observation.visible_scene: A blue faceted pear/oval-cut gemstone is held by four thin curved metal prongs mounted on a short cylindrical metal base (a ring/stone holder), set against a uniform featureless gray background. The clip is a temporally cropped excerpt; the holder and gem are already in motion at the first frame and remain in motion at the last.
visible_changes: The gem-and-prong assembly slowly rotates about a roughly vertical axis: the four prongs reposition relative to the camera (the prong that crosses the front of the stone in early frames moves to the side in later frames, and the left/right curved prongs swap which side they dominate), and the gem's outline tilts as it turns.
Bright green and cyan sparkle flashes appear, move, and vanish across the gem's facets from frame to frame, tracking the rotation rather than indicating separate objects.
The whole object drifts gradually to the right within the frame: the gem's projected center and the prong tips sit noticeably further right in the last frames than in the first.
The apparent viewing angle of the cylindrical base changes: early frames show the base's open top seen from above, while later frames show more of its ridged/threaded side wall seen more edge-on.
The gray background stays static and unchanged throughout.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the rotation is a continuous mechanical spin or a hand-turned motion (no operator or tool is visible).
What happens before t=0 and after the last frame; the excerpt neither starts nor completes the rotation.
The gem's material identity and the holder's purpose are not determinable from the frames.
uncertain_details: The rightward drift and the change in base tilt could be camera movement (pan/tilt) or actual object movement; with a uniform background this cannot be resolved, so both are reported as relative changes only.
It is not fully clear whether the gem rotates independently of the prongs or the entire assembly rotates together; the prong repositioning suggests the whole top rotates.
Exact rotation direction and angle per interval are not reliably measurable from the sampled frames.

may already be underway in the first view and may continue beyond the last. The endpoints need
NOT match or connect as a loop. Do not judge different endpoints as a physical inconsistency,
and do not invent a trigger, contact, start, stop, landing, disappearance or completion to make
the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.
If an editing cut is visible inside the segment, distinguish it from continuous physical motion;
do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.
Describe what is visible during the excerpt, the actual changes, and supported persistent
properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;
do not invent causes, an earlier impact, an unseen operator, material identities or later outcomes.
Do not infer motion from one frame, a visible seam or a single pose. Static intervals are valid.
Do not supply named physics laws. Compare each important entity's first and last image positions
and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
Return JSON {"visible_scene":"...", "visible_changes":["observation supported within the excerpt"],
"outside_clip_unknowns":["unseen prerequisites or outcomes, only when relevant"],
"uncertain_details":["..."]}. Be concrete and concise, in English. This is not a complete event reconstruction.
